To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the behavioral and neural signatures of common activities of daily living were accompanied by differing biomarkers.
walking while talking and texting are associated with decreased gait performance, and that these conditions are accompanied by differing frequency specific neural “biomarker” signatures.

the neural biomarkers for dual tasking while walking in real-life scenarios are frequency-specific and that the neural biomarker for texting while walking is a decrease in beta neural power in the frontal-premotor area.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the neural biomarkers that are present during the performance of common real-life walking activities.
how the brain and body work together to produce human movement in real-world settings.
the neural biomarkers that are associated with common real-life activities.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the behavioral signatures of common real-life walking activities performed in an ecological setting were accompanied by frequency specific neural biomarkers.

walking while conversing is associated with increased neural power in the left-frontal and the right parietal areas, while walking while texting is associated with decreased β power in a cluster over the frontal-pre-motor and sensorimotor regions.
the current study demonstrates that the neural correlates of walking while conversing and while texting with a mobile phone are different.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have shown the neural and kinematic signatures of walking whilst performing a cognitive task, which is a common activity in the real-world, in healthy adults.
we have identified a set of neural biomarkers that can be used to describe gait performance in healthy individuals.
the neural correlates of single- and dual-task walking are condition-specific, and can be captured by MoBI.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we have shown the feasibility of using MoBI technologies to study the neural and behavioral aspects of walking in the real world.
the MoBI approach can be applied to study the neural underpinnings of gait control in ecologically valid scenarios.
we can now study how the human brain and body interact in the real world, in real-time, and with a high spatial and temporal resolution.
